opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a pretty useful analogy, because a lot of the intuitions we've developed from training models carry over surprisingly well to how you think about people and organizations.

If you manage a team in a purely "SFT" way, you're essentially giving people demonstrations: here's exactly how to do it, follow these steps, imitate this example. That works well when the task is well-defined and you already know what the right answer looks like. It's efficient, it reduces variance, and for someone new it's often the fastest way to get them up to a reasonable baseline. But the ceiling is limited. If everyone is just imitating the manager, the team can never really be better than the manager. You're bounded by the quality of your demonstrations.

The "RL" approach is different. You don't tell people exactly what to do; you define the objective clearly, you give them a reward signal, and you let them explore. The beauty of that is people can discover solutions you never would have thought of. In research especially, that's where the real breakthroughs come from. Many of the most interesting things in our field didn't come from someone following a playbook. They came from someone being given room to try things, fail, and try again, with a clear sense of what "good" means.

But RL has its own failure modes, and they map onto management too. The first is reward hacking. If you define the objective badly, people will optimize the metric rather than the thing you actually care about, and that's not their fault; it's the fault of whoever designed the reward. So a big part of a leader's job in an RL-style organization is really reward design: making sure the goals are aligned with what actually matters, not just what's easy to measure. The second is that pure exploration from scratch is very inefficient. If you throw someone into a hard problem with zero prior, they may wander around for a long time without signal.

So in practice I think the answer is similar to what works for models: you want a good prior, and then you do RL on top of it. You use something like SFT to establish shared context, taste, and basic standards, so people have a reasonable starting policy. Then, as much as possible, you shift to setting goals and giving feedback rather than prescribing actions. And the more capable and senior the people are, the more you should lean toward RL. With really strong people, micromanaging is like overfitting them to your own demonstrations; you're throwing away their capability.

I'd also add one thing. In RL, the quality of the environment matters a lot. For a team, the environment is the culture: whether people get honest feedback quickly, whether failure is tolerated when it's a reasonable bet, whether information flows freely. If the environment is good, people learn fast and generalize. If it's noisy or political, the reward signal gets corrupted and people learn the wrong things. So I spend a lot of my thinking not on telling people what to do, but on trying to make the environment and the objectives right, and then trusting the team to find the path.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using SFT to establish shared context, taste, and basic standards, then applying RL on top.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun analogy, and I actually think about it this way quite a lot.

Supervised fine-tuning is when you give people the answer directly. You show them exactly what good looks like, you correct them step by step, and they imitate. It's very efficient early on. When someone just joins the team, or when the task is well understood and you already know the right way to do it, SFT is the right tool. You don't want a new engineer rediscovering how to set up the training pipeline through trial and error. Just show them.

But the problem with SFT is the same problem you see in models. You get a ceiling. The person can only ever be as good as the demonstrations you gave them. They learn to match your distribution, not to exceed it. And if you over-fit them on your way of doing things, you lose the diversity that actually makes a team strong. You end up with a bunch of copies of yourself, which sounds nice until you realize your own blind spots are now everyone's blind spots.

Reinforcement learning is different. You don't tell people how to do it. You define the reward, you make the objective very clear, and then you let them explore. They will try things you would never have tried. Some of those things fail, and that's fine. Some of them work much better than what you would have done. That's where the real upside comes from. The best results we've had internally almost always came from someone who was given a hard, clear goal and the space to find their own path to it.

The catch is that RL is expensive and unstable. If the reward is badly specified, people optimize the wrong thing. You see reward hacking in organizations all the time, people hitting the metric and missing the point. And exploration has a cost. Someone can spend two months going down a direction that doesn't work. So you need a strong signal, you need relatively fast feedback loops, and you need enough trust that failure isn't punished, otherwise people stop exploring and quietly revert to imitation.

So my honest answer is that it's a curriculum, not a choice. Early on, and for things that are solved problems, you do more SFT. Then you deliberately shift the mixture toward RL as people build a good enough base. The job of a manager becomes less about providing demonstrations and more about designing the reward, keeping the objective clean, and making sure the feedback arrives quickly enough that learning actually happens.

And one more thing I'd add. The most valuable people are the ones for whom the reward function is already internalized. You don't need to specify much. You just point at the problem. For those people, any amount of SFT from me is probably a net negative. The best thing I can do is get out of the way.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a curriculum that uses more SFT early, then shifts toward RL as team members build a foundation.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful analogy. Supervised fine-tuning is like showing someone how you would do the work: here’s an example, here’s the process, here’s what a good result looks like. Reinforcement learning is more like giving them a goal and feedback, then letting them discover how to get there.

For someone who’s new to a team, examples can be very helpful. If you only say, “Go achieve this outcome,” they may spend a lot of time rediscovering things you could have taught them. But if you keep prescribing every step, you limit what they can contribute. They might find a better approach than yours.

So I’d use enough guidance to establish a shared understanding, then give people room to explore. The difficult part is the feedback: are you rewarding something that actually matters, or just something that’s easy to measure? In research especially, a good decision can produce a negative result. You want people to learn from that, rather than learn to avoid taking risks.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using examples and guidance to establish shared understanding, then giving people room to explore—combining SFT-like guidance with RL-like goals and feedback.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of supervised fine-tuning as showing people what good work looks like. You give examples, explain your reasoning, and help them build a shared understanding of the standard. That’s especially useful when someone is new or when the task is unfamiliar.

Reinforcement learning is more like giving people ownership of a problem, letting them try different approaches, and providing feedback on the results. You specify what you’re trying to achieve, but you don’t prescribe every step.

The balance depends on how well someone understands the context. If you only give examples, people may learn to imitate you without developing their own judgment. If you only reward outcomes, they may spend a lot of time discovering things you could have explained—or optimize for a metric that doesn’t capture what you actually want.

So I would start with enough guidance to establish the fundamentals, then give people increasing freedom. And when something goes wrong, ask whether they needed a better example, clearer feedback, or a clearer objective. Those are different management problems.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting with guidance and examples (SFT-like) before giving people increasing freedom (RL-like), combining both approaches.
